title: Uniform truncation maps for families under a functor of finite amplitude
statement:
Let $\mathcal A,\mathcal B$ be Grothendieck abelian categories in a fixed universe [def-sp-grothendieck-abelian], with ordinary unbounded derived categories $D(\mathcal A),D(\mathcal B)$ [def-weil-abstract-derived-category]. Let $\mathcal P$ be an isomorphism-invariant class of objects of $\mathcal A$ containing zero and closed under small coproducts. Let $G:D(\mathcal A)\to D(\mathcal B)$ be an exact triangulated functor commuting with integer shifts [def-weil-triangulated-category]. Suppose $c\in\mathbf N$, $G(D^{\ge a})\subset D^{\ge a}$ for every integer $a$, and $G(L)\in D^{\le b+c}$ whenever $L\in D^{\le b}$ and every $H^j(L)$ belongs to $\mathcal P$. Bounds use the standard t-structures [def-sbc-standard-tstructure-derived-category]. For any small family $(K_s)_{s\in I}$ with all $H^j(K_s)\in\mathcal P$, and integer $m$, put
$$U_s=\tau_{\le m}K_s,\quad u_s:U_s\to K_s,\qquad V_s=\tau_{\ge m-c}U_s,\quad v_s:U_s\to V_s,$$
using the canonical good truncation maps [def-kun-truncations]. Then every $V_s$ has $\mathcal P$-cohomology in the common interval $[m-c,m]$, and each of the following four maps is invertible in $\mathcal B$:
$$H^m(G(\bigoplus_su_s)),\quad H^m(G(\bigoplus_sv_s)),\quad H^m(\bigoplus_sG(u_s)),\quad H^m(\bigoplus_sG(v_s)).$$
Here all sums are ambient derived coproducts, and $\bigoplus_su_s$ and $\bigoplus_sv_s$ denote the maps induced by the specified coprojections. The assertions are natural in the family $(K_s)$, include the empty family, and require no common cohomological bound on the $K_s$.

proof.text: For either $\mathcal C=\mathcal A$ or $\mathcal B$, small coproducts preserve finite limits. Indeed, the coproduct functor on $I$-indexed families is the filtered colimit, over the finite subsets $J\subseteq I$, of the finite subcoproduct functors. Each finite subcoproduct is a finite product in the abelian category and therefore preserves finite limits. The filtered-colimit functor preserves finite limits by the cited Grothendieck lemma. The identification with the coproduct follows from its universal property: a compatible collection of maps from the finite subsums is exactly one map from each summand. This also covers $I=\varnothing$, whose finite-subset poset has its single empty object. Thus coproducts are exact colimits in both categories.

proof.text: By the termwise-derived-coproduct theorem, representatives $L_s^\bullet$ compute every ambient coproduct in $D(\mathcal C)$, with the specified coprojections. Apply preservation of exact colimits by complex homology, using step 1 and the factorization of cohomology through localization. For every integer $j$ this gives the canonical natural isomorphism $\theta_L^j:\bigoplus_s H^j(L_s)\xrightarrow{\sim}H^j(\bigoplus_sL_s)$. For every family $h_s:L_s\to L_s^{\prime}$ its defining coprojection identities give $H^j(\bigoplus_sh_s)\theta_L^j=\theta_{L^{\prime}}^j(\bigoplus_sH^j(h_s))$. In particular, a coproduct retains any common cohomological upper or lower bound. In $\mathcal A$, it also retains $\mathcal P$-cohomology, since $\mathcal P$ is closed under coproducts and isomorphisms.

proof.text: Set $a=m-c$. Good truncations retain the original cohomology in their retained degrees and have zero cohomology elsewhere. Consequently $U_s$, $V_s$, and $T_s=\tau_{\le a-1}U_s$ have $\mathcal P$-cohomology: this uses only isomorphism invariance and $0\in\mathcal P$. Moreover $U_s\in D^{\le m}$, $V_s\in D^{\ge a}\cap D^{\le m}$, and $T_s\in D^{\le a-1}$. This proves the asserted common interval for $V_s$; $c\ge0$ gives $a\le m$. By step 2 the sums of these families have the same respective bounds and $\mathcal P$-cohomology.

proof.text: The canonical truncation maps commute with ambient coproducts. To check the maps as well as the objects, choose complex representatives. Step 1 supplies the finite-limit hypothesis of the arrow-kernel/cokernel lemma, so $\bigoplus_s\ker d_s^m\cong\ker(\bigoplus_sd_s^m)$ and $\bigoplus_s\operatorname{coker}d_s^{a-1}\cong\operatorname{coker}(\bigoplus_sd_s^{a-1})$, with their canonical kernel inclusions and cokernel projections. The formulas for good truncation now give natural complex isomorphisms, hence derived isomorphisms $\alpha:\bigoplus_sU_s\xrightarrow{\sim}\tau_{\le m}(\bigoplus_sK_s)$ and $\beta:\bigoplus_sV_s\xrightarrow{\sim}\tau_{\ge a}(\bigoplus_sU_s)$. Degreewise the maps away from the boundary are identities or zero, and at the boundary they are precisely those inclusions or projections. Therefore $u_{\oplus K}\alpha=\bigoplus_su_s$ and $\beta(\bigoplus_sv_s)=v_{\oplus U}$, where $u_L:\tau_{\le m}L\to L$ and $v_L:L\to\tau_{\ge a}L$ are the canonical arrows.

proof.text: For any $L\in D(\mathcal A)$, the canonical triangle is $\tau_{\le m}L\xrightarrow{u_L}L\to W\to(\tau_{\le m}L)[1]$, with $W=\tau_{\ge m+1}L\in D^{\ge m+1}$. Exactness of $G$ makes its image distinguished. The lower-bound hypothesis gives $G(W)\in D^{\ge m+1}$. Thus the long exact cohomology sequence has segment $0=H^{m-1}(G(W))\to H^m(G(\tau_{\le m}L))\xrightarrow{H^m(G(u_L))}H^m(G(L))\to H^m(G(W))=0$. Its middle map is both monic and epic, hence invertible in the abelian category. Apply this with $L=K_s$ for each $s$, and also with $L=\bigoplus_sK_s$.

source.place: Tag 08J5, remark-truncation-distinguished-triangle, at m; Tags 05RS and 0147, cohomology long exact sequence

proof.text: For any $L$ with $\mathcal P$-cohomology, the other canonical triangle is $T\to L\xrightarrow{v_L}\tau_{\ge a}L\to T[1]$, where $T=\tau_{\le a-1}L$. Its cohomology is either that of $L$ or zero, so it belongs to $\mathcal P$, and $T\in D^{\le a-1}$. The upper-amplitude hypothesis therefore gives $G(T)\in D^{\le a-1+c}=D^{\le m-1}$. Apply $G$ and use the long exact sequence: $0=H^m(G(T))\to H^m(G(L))\xrightarrow{H^m(G(v_L))}H^m(G(\tau_{\ge a}L))\to H^{m+1}(G(T))=0$. Again the middle map is invertible. Apply this with $L=U_s$ and with $L=\bigoplus_sU_s$, whose $\mathcal P$-cohomology was checked in steps 2-3. No closure of $\mathcal P$ under extensions or subquotients is used.

proof.text: The two pre-$G$ sum assertions now follow with the actual specified arrows. Step 4 gives $G(\bigoplus_su_s)=G(u_{\oplus K})G(\alpha)$, so step 5 and invertibility of $\alpha$ imply invertibility of $H^m(G(\bigoplus_su_s))$. Likewise $G(\beta)G(\bigoplus_sv_s)=G(v_{\oplus U})$; step 6 and invertibility of $\beta$ imply invertibility of $H^m(G(\bigoplus_sv_s))$. This uses only functoriality and composition/cancellation of isomorphisms.

proof.text: For the two post-$G$ sum assertions, apply step 2 in $\mathcal B$ to the families $G(u_s)$ and $G(v_s)$. Under the canonical isomorphisms $\theta$, their degree-$m$ cohomology maps are respectively $\bigoplus_sH^m(G(u_s))$ and $\bigoplus_sH^m(G(v_s))$. Steps 5-6 make every summand invertible. The coproduct of the inverses is an inverse to each displayed coproduct map, as is checked on every coprojection. Conjugating by $\theta$ proves invertibility of $H^m(\bigoplus_sG(u_s))$ and $H^m(\bigoplus_sG(v_s))$.

proof.text: All constructions used are natural in a morphism of $I$-indexed families: good truncation acts by the induced maps on kernels and cokernels, its canonical arrows are natural, and all coproduct maps and comparisons are determined by their coprojections. Applying $G$ and $H^m$ preserves these commuting squares, and inverses of the resulting natural isomorphisms are natural as well. For $I=\varnothing$ the coproducts are zero; an additive exact functor takes a zero object to a zero object, since it takes its identity, which is zero, to an identity which is zero. Thus all four maps are isomorphisms also then. The argument used no bound on the original $K_s$ and only the fixed integers $m,c$.
